नरनारायणाभ्यां तु जगतो हितकाम्यया।
तथानुष्ठीयते मूलधर्मो वदरिकाश्रमे ।
एषः प्रकृतिधर्माख्यो वासुदेवैकगोचरः ॥

The same text characterizes the Sāttvata-vidhi or
Vāsudeva-mata as ‘ekāyana-veda’ (viz. the Veda which is
the only path to salvation) (1,56). Puruṣottama-saṃhitā
(1,12) also proclaims that this is the only way, and that
there is no other.

श्रुणुध्वं मुनयः सर्वे वेदमेकायनाभिदम्।
मोक्षायनाय वै पन्थाः एतदन्यो न विद्यते ।
तस्मादेकायनं चेति प्रवदन्ति मनीषिणः ॥

Śrī-praśna-saṃhitā (2,38-39) explains that Pāñcarātra
is the path that leads to the salvation of individuals; that
this path takes the -form of worship of Godhead; and that
this is the ageless path shown in the Vedic corpus.
According to this text, the Pāñcarātra rests on the head
of the Vedas (i.e. is superior to the Vedas).

वेदमेकायनं नाम वेदानां शिरसि स्थितम्।
तदर्थकं पांचरात्रं मोक्षदं तत्क्रियावहम्।।
यस्मिन्नेको मोक्षमार्गः वेदे प्रोक्तः सनातनः ।

summary: This section introduces the Pāñcarātra tradition, also known as Sāttvata-vidhi or Vāsudeva-mata, as the theological background for the Bhāgavata. It traces its origin to the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa and its propagation by Vāsudeva. Citing various Samhitās (Puruṣottama, Śrī-praśna, Vāmana), the text argues that Pāñcarātra is the 'ekāyana-veda,' the singular and exclusive path to salvation (mokṣa). Furthermore, it asserts the supremacy of the Pāñcarātra over the traditional Vedic corpus, claiming it "rests on the head of the Vedas" and is uniquely focused on salvation through the worship of Godhead.
main_arguments: The Pāñcarātra path, originating from Nara and Nārāyaṇa, is the 'ekāyana-veda' — the one and only path to salvation.
This tradition, propagated by Vāsudeva, is not merely a part of the Vedic tradition but is theologically superior to it.
Various Pāñcarātra texts, such as the Puruṣottama, Śrī-praśna, and Vāmana Samhitās, consistently affirm this exclusive and supreme status.
Unlike the broader Vedic scriptures, the Pāñcarātra system is singularly focused on salvation as its ultimate and only goal.
methodology: The author employs a textual and exegetical methodology. The argument is constructed by citing and interpreting specific Sanskrit verses from several primary texts of the Pāñcarātra tradition (Puruṣottama-saṃhitā, Śrī-praśna-saṃhitā, Vāmana-saṃhitā). This approach uses the tradition's own scriptural sources to define its core tenets, its relationship with the Vedas, and its ultimate soteriological aim.
historiographical_context: The text operates within the academic and theological study of Vaiṣṇavism, specifically addressing the historical and doctrinal relationship between the Pāñcarātra school and the orthodox Vedic tradition. The argument for Pāñcarātra's superiority over the Vedas reflects an internal, sectarian viewpoint common in theological literature, where a tradition seeks to establish its own authority and primacy over the established scriptural canon (śruti). This positioning is a key element in understanding the development and self-perception of sectarian Hindu traditions.
research_questions: What are the origins and core principles of the Pāñcarātra (or Sāttvata) tradition?
How do Pāñcarātra texts define their own authority in relation to the Vedas?
What is the ultimate goal of the Pāñcarātra path according to its own scriptures?
How does this Pāñcarātra background inform the theology of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa?
book_structure_overview: This page does not provide an overview of the entire book's structure. It functions as the beginning of a chapter or section that establishes the Pāñcarātra theological framework. The structure of this specific section is a series of theological claims, each substantiated by direct quotations from different Samhitā texts, logically building the case for the Pāñcarātra's supreme and exclusive soteriological status as a prelude to discussing the Bhāgavata.
